If you only remember one thing: Open A I shipped G P T six Astra on Thursday, called it the start of the A G I era, and the same day two members of Congress moved to make building superintelligence a crime. Capability and backlash arrived together.

Section one. G P T six Astra, and the busiest launch week of the year. This is from your Reads: The Rundown, A I News by swyx, and That One A I.

Open A I launched G P T six Astra on September third. The company calls it the world's most intelligent and aligned model. It rolls out first to a limited set of organizations, then to Chat G P T Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise, the A P I, Azure and Bedrock. Price: ten dollars per million input tokens, fifty dollars per million output tokens. Context window just over one million tokens.

Swyx's verdict in A I News: new state of the art on computer use and coding. Two and a half times pricier per token, but way cheaper per task. His Latent Space post frames it as an automated A I engineer you can hire for under six dollars an hour.

The safety headline. Astra is Open A I's first broadly deployed model to hit the Critical cybersecurity threshold under its Preparedness Framework. That means it can, in some conditions, find unknown vulnerabilities and develop exploits without continuous human direction. Open A I added tighter internal isolation, encrypted checkpoints and expanded monitoring.

The monitorability worry. The Information reported that Astra uses a technique called recurrent depth, looping over the same text repeatedly. It boosts performance, but produces reasoning that's harder to read. Open A I says it dialed the loops back so Astra still shows its work. Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said he wants to prevent a race into unmonitorability.

And the rest of launch week. Anthropic's Claude Fable five point one went generally available on September first, at the same ten and fifty dollar pricing, and it can run your computer. Google shipped Gemini three point eight Flash on September second, plus a defenders only Cyber variant. DeepMind's Koray Kavukcuoglu admitted Gemini sits a little below the frontier. Meta shipped Muse Spark one point three at roughly ten cents per million tokens. Zuckerberg called it frontier performance almost too cheap to meter. It now trails only Fable five point one and Opus five on the Artificial Analysis index, and a bigger model codenamed Watermelon is next.

Why it matters: the frontier moved from chat to autonomous professional work in a single week, and the safety story, cyber capability and reasoning you can't read, is now inseparable from the capability story.

Section two. A I policy: the superintelligence ban bill.

On September third, Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. It would permanently prohibit developing or deploying superintelligent A I, pause advanced A I development until a federal regulator sets safety rules, create a cabinet level A I agency, and direct the U S to pursue international agreements. The penalty for building superintelligence: up to twenty years in prison. That's the same as nuclear weapons development. Slim odds of passing, but it shifts the Washington debate from copyright and jobs to whether some capabilities should exist at all.

Is Europe converging? E U tech chief Henna Virkkunen, at the G twenty innovation summit in North Carolina, argued the U S is quietly building E U style guardrails through state laws, courts and national security rules, just not through one big act.

China enforcement. Beijing says it removed five point six million pieces of content and hit forty nine thousand accounts in a nationwide campaign against A I misuse: deepfakes, impersonation, and content affecting minors.

Also: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Axios, we trust Anthropic, saying the company is back on the right side of its relationship with government. And New York City public schools are banning A I through eighth grade, per The Rundown.

Coming up: Brazil's Senate votes on its A I bill September sixteenth. California's governor has until September thirtieth to sign or veto S B ten forty seven.

Why it matters: regulators are no longer asking whether to regulate frontier A I. They're arguing over which capabilities cross a red line, and who enforces it.
